Visiting Researcher and Instructor


Designed and delivered undergraduate courses in causal inference, research design, and statistical methods. Led survey-based research projects on public policy preferences. Managed a multi-institutional survey experiment evaluating behavioural interventions for childhood vaccination uptake, collaborating with researchers at the University of Oxford and the Technical University of Munich.




Australian National University, Canberra · 2019 – 2025


Doctoral Researcher and Teaching Assistant


Designed and conducted original quantitative research using experimental methods and meta-analysis. Published peer-reviewed research in Royal Society Open Science, Nature, and Nature Human Behaviour. Facilitated weekly tutorial sessions in quantitative methods and research design.






Quantitative Analysis: Experimental design, causal inference, econometrics, survey methodology, policy and impact evaluation
Programming & Data Tools: R, Python, SQL, Stata, Excel, Git
Structured Problem-Solving: Evidence synthesis, meta-analysis, analytical framework development for complex policy questions
Presentation & Reporting: PowerPoint, LaTeX, Quarto, publication-quality data visualisation
Communication: Academic publishing, technical writing, teaching and facilitation, stakeholder briefings
Languages: Cebuano (second-most-spoken Philippine language)

title: Statistical Consulting
text:
I provide statistical consulting services to academic researchers, policy organisations, and international institutions. My work spans research design, data analysis, and methodological review.




RWI – Leibniz Institute · Open Philanthropy (Apr 2024–Nov 2025)


Maternal Health Outcomes Under a Conditional Cash Transfer Program


Evaluated the robustness of a randomised controlled trial assessing a cash transfer intervention on maternal health, delivering analytical findings to inform philanthropic investment decisions.




Monash University (Jan 2024–May 2025)


Trade and Financial Openness Panel Data Analysis


Conducted panel data econometric analysis of country-level trade and financial openness indicators for a project funded by the Office of National Intelligence.




KIMEP University · Presidential Administration of Kazakhstan (2022)


Conjoint Experiment for Public Attitudes to Foreign Policy and Political Reform


Designed and analysed a conjoint survey experiment to inform a policy reform report on economic, political, and educational priorities, prepared for the Presidential Administration of the Republic of Kazakhstan.




Center for Open Science (2022)


Robustness and Replicability Research


Contributed quantitative analysis to a large-scale international collaboration evaluating analytical robustness across the social and behavioural sciences co-authored in Nature.

title: About me
text:
Welcome! I recently completed my PhD in Political Science at the Australian National University, specialising in political behaviour.
My PhD research focused on using survey experiments and meta-analytic methods to understand why voters in democracies sometimes support or tolerate illiberal and undemocratic politicians, how they might be persuaded to vote pro-democratically, and which democracies are most at risk of democratic decline. I investigated how providing voters with information about politicians’ undemocratic positions affects their electoral choices in newer and long-standing democracies.1
Beyond political behaviour, I have a strong interest in research credibility and behavioural public policy. My work on data availability and research transparency in approximately 20,000 quantitative political science and international relations publications was published by Royal Society Open Science in 2024. I have also served as a coauthor and statistical analyst on several large-scale research collaborations on social science replicability and robustness, which include the Center for Open Science’s SCORE project (Multi100), published in Nature, and RWI Essen’s Robustness and Replicability in Economics (R2E) project – funded by Open Philanthropy.2
While in Kazakhstan, my collaboration with the Trust in Science and Science-related Populism (TISP) cross-national, Many Labs project, whose main findings have been published in Nature Human Behaviour, prompted my colleagues and I to investigate the the efficacy of MMR vaccine communication strategies in Kazakhstan’s low scientific trust environment.3
